name: Just-in-time context loading / agentic retrieval patterns
publisher: Cross-cutting technique synthesized across multiple publishers: Anthropic (Effective context engineering for AI agents, Sept 2025, and the separate Managing context on the Claude Developer Platform / context-editing + memory tool launch post, also Sept 2025), LangChain (Context Engineering for Agents, July 2025; How agents can use filesystems for context engineering, Nov 2025), Drew Breunig (independent, June 2025, under the 'Offloading' and 'RAG' tactics), Philipp Schmid (Google DeepMind, personal blog), plus secondary vendor explainers (TrueFoundry, Sourcegraph, Elastic, dev.to) that repackage the same pattern under the 'JIT context' label.
date_published: Earliest clear articulation under this name: Anthropic, 2025-09-29 ('maintain lightweight identifiers... load data into context at runtime'). The underlying mechanism was already named by Breunig on 2025-06-26 as 'Context Offloading' and by LangChain on 2025-07-02 as the 'Select' strategy; secondary vendor posts applying the 'just-in-time' label specifically post-date Anthropic's piece (late 2025 into 2026).
source_type: practitioner framework (synthesized across vendor blogs and one independent practitioner essay; no single primary source owns this technique)
claim_value: The technique: instead of pre-loading all potentially relevant data into the context window up front, an agent keeps small, cheap references (file paths, stored queries, URLs, document IDs, database handles) in context and uses tools (file read, bash grep/head/tail, a search call, a DB query) to pull the actual content in only at the moment it is needed, then can discard or re-summarize it afterward. Anthropic frames this as mirroring how humans use filing systems and bookmarks rather than memorizing full corpora. Concretely cited implementations: Claude Code uses the pattern to analyze large datasets by writing targeted queries and using Bash (head/tail) instead of loading full files into context. LangChain's filesystem post and Deep Agents SDK operationalize the same idea as agent filesystem tools (ls/glob/grep/read_file), explicitly citing Manus's 'recitation/filesystem' pattern and Cursor's search architecture as prior art. No independently-run A/B benchmark comparing JIT loading against up-front loading, holding task and model constant, was found anywhere in this research pass; the quantitative evidence that exists (Anthropic's 39% improvement / 84% token reduction figures) belongs to a different, related Anthropic feature (context editing + memory tool) rather than to JIT retrieval itself, and even that figure is a single-vendor, single-task (100-turn web search) internal eval, not an independently replicated benchmark.
claim_definition: This is a practitioner technique recommendation repeated across several non-academic sources, not a benchmark result or a formal ablation study. No source in this set runs a controlled experiment isolating 'JIT retrieval' as the only variable against a 'load everything up front' baseline on the same task/model; the supporting evidence is instead (a) anecdotal description of how Claude Code or Deep Agents are built, (b) the indirect, mechanistic case made by Lost in the Middle / NoLiMa / Context Rot that stuffing more tokens into context degrades performance (which argues against up-front loading in general but was not designed to test JIT retrieval specifically), and (c) a numeric result (39%/84%) that is real but belongs to a sibling feature (context editing/compaction + memory tool), not to JIT retrieval as such, despite being informally attached to the 'context engineering' narrative that includes JIT retrieval.
evidence_category: practitioner anecdote and architectural description, reinforced by adjacent (not directly on-point) benchmark results about long-context degradation; no dedicated benchmark/empirical result isolates JIT retrieval itself
reproducibility: Not reproducible in the benchmark sense: there is no public eval harness that specifically measures 'JIT retrieval vs. up-front context stuffing' holding everything else constant. What is public and runnable: LangChain's archived langchain-ai/how_to_fix_your_context notebooks implement related tactics (RAG, offloading, pruning) individually, and Anthropic's memory-tool/context-editing feature has its own (vendor-reported) 100-turn web-search eval, but that eval measures compaction/memory, not JIT retrieval in isolation. The closest genuine empirical support is indirect: Lost in the Middle (Liu et al., peer-reviewed, independently replicated), NoLiMa (ICML 2025, independently reused), and Context Rot (Chroma, reproducible via public MIT-licensed repo but not yet independently replicated by a third party) all show that longer, more fully-loaded contexts degrade model accuracy, which is consistent with JIT retrieval being a reasonable mitigation but does not directly test it.
publisher_sells_relevant_product: Mixed, and this matters for how the technique is being pushed. Anthropic sells Claude/Claude Code and a memory-tool/context-editing product feature that operationalizes a close cousin of JIT retrieval; LangChain sells LangGraph, LangSmith, and the Deep Agents SDK, whose filesystem tools are explicitly pitched as the productized implementation of JIT retrieval; secondary explainers (TrueFoundry, Elastic, Sourcegraph) each sell adjacent infrastructure (ML platform, search/relevance engine, code intelligence) and use the JIT framing to argue for their own retrieval/relevance tooling. Breunig (the independent originator of the underlying 'Offloading' tactic) sells nothing and has no product stake.
conflict_notes: The specific 39% improvement / 84% token reduction figures that circulate attached to 'Anthropic's context engineering advice' (and sometimes to JIT retrieval specifically, since both appear in the same September 2025 cluster of Anthropic posts) actually belong to a separate post, 'Managing context on the Claude Developer Platform,' about the context-editing and memory-tool features, not to the 'Effective context engineering for AI agents' essay where JIT retrieval is named and defined, and not to JIT retrieval as an isolated variable. Confirmed again in this pass via web search: context editing alone gave 29% improvement, context editing + memory tool gave 39%, and the 84% token reduction was measured on a 100-turn web-search eval, none of which isolates the just-in-time-retrieval tactic from compaction/memory. Citing these numbers as evidence 'JIT retrieval works' overstates what was actually measured.
relationship: Supports the context-engineering narrative as its single most concrete, implementable piece of advice (it is literally the first fully mechanical technique Anthropic names that a developer can go build), but the evidence base behind it is weaker than its prominence suggests: it is presented confidently across every source in this set as self-evidently correct, while the actual empirical support is either anecdotal (Claude Code 'uses this pattern') or borrowed from adjacent-but-distinct findings (long-context degradation studies, a different feature's eval numbers). This is worth flagging for a piece arguing that context engineering's 'main actionable advance' runs ahead of its evidence.
derivative_of: Substantively, this is retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) under agentic control, not a new invention. RAG (Lewis et al. 2020 and the broader RAG literature) already established the core move: don't put the whole corpus in the prompt, retrieve the relevant slice at query time. What 'just-in-time context loading' adds, and it is a real but incremental addition, is (a) applying that retrieve-at-the-moment-of-need logic to an agent's own working state (tool outputs, prior turns, file contents), not just an external knowledge corpus, and (b) giving the agent itself the tool-calling agency to decide when and what to retrieve, rather than a fixed retrieval step hard-wired before generation. LangChain's own taxonomy folds JIT retrieval into its 'Select' strategy, one of four, alongside Write/Compress/Isolate, and credits Breunig's 'Offloading' and classic 'RAG' tactics as the direct lineage. So: real technique, genuinely useful, but best described as RAG generalized to agent-internal state and put under the agent's own tool-use control, rather than a substantively new retrieval paradigm.
register: practitioner/engineer primarily, across every source in this synthesis (Anthropic's engineering blog, LangChain's blog, Breunig's essay, secondary vendor explainers); none of this is pitched at enterprise IT buyers or academic researchers specifically, in contrast to the survey-stat vendor reports elsewhere in this research set.
confidence: secondary_unverified (as a cross-cutting synthesis). The individual claims about who said what and when are primary_verified (already confirmed in the Anthropic, LangChain, and Breunig items this synthesis draws on), but the composite claim examined here, that JIT retrieval has been shown to work better than up-front loading, is unverified: no source in this set or found in additional search provides a controlled comparison.
notes: The discrepancy worth carrying into any essay: 'just-in-time context loading' is presented industry-wide as context engineering's signature actionable technique, with real adoption (Claude Code, LangChain's Deep Agents SDK, Manus, Cursor all described as using some version of it), but the case for it rests on architecture description and adjacent degradation benchmarks (Lost in the Middle, NoLiMa, Context Rot) rather than a direct test of JIT vs. up-front loading. The 39%/84% Anthropic figures that often get attached to this story belong to a sibling feature (context editing/memory tool), which several secondary explainers blur together with JIT retrieval. Treat the technique as plausible and widely adopted, but not as benchmark-proven relative to the alternative it claims to beat.
already_cited: no - not referenced by name in article_ideas.md's 09-27 'Context engineering didn't retire the prompt' entry or the AGENTS.md thought.
new_angle: Gives the planned piece its sharpest 'is this actually new' finding: just-in-time context loading is the one technique every source in this research set converges on as context engineering's real, implementable contribution, yet (1) it is RAG applied to agent-internal state under the agent's own tool-calling control rather than a new retrieval paradigm, (2) the headline quantitative support circulating for it (39%/84%) is misattributed, it belongs to a different Anthropic feature (context editing + memory tool), not to JIT retrieval in isolation, and (3) no source, vendor or academic, has run a direct controlled comparison of JIT retrieval against up-front loading; the supporting evidence is architectural anecdote plus adjacent long-context-degradation benchmarks that were not designed to test this specific claim. This lets the piece credit the technique as sensible and widely adopted while being precise that 'works better than up-front loading' is asserted, not measured.
